newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal gears up for public sector wage round.
newsitem.headline: Portugal gears up for public sector wage round.

text.p: Public sector wage increases next year must be below the 4.25 percent agreed for 1996 as tight control of state spending is essential for Portugal's hopes of joining a single European currency, a senior official said.

The Socialist government must by law begin the 1997 round of wage talks with civil servant unions before it presents its budget proposals to parliament on October 15, said Arnaldo Silva, the government's number two wage negotiator.
He said he hoped the talks, due to begin in the coming days, would be concluded by December.

"Everything indicates that the 1997 wage increases should be less than 1996," Silva, who works alongside Assistant Minister to the Prime Minister Jorge Coelho in public sector wage negotiations, told Reuters in an interview on Thursday.
"The unions know that the wage increases for 1997 can't be as generous as those for 1996. We are hoping that union demands come down," he added.

The government of Prime Minister Antonio Guterres, which took office in November 1995, set 1996 public sector wage increases at 4.25 percent, slightly above inflation, after talks with unions lasting several months.
The government wants inflation down by December 1997 to 2.25-2.50 percent from a forecast 3.0 percent at end-1996.
Three public sector trade union groups representing an estimated 500,000 to 800,000 civil servants were demanding 1997 wage increases of between 4.5 and seven percent, Silva said.
This was below their initial demands of between 6.5 and 11.5 percent in the 1996 wages round.

"We all know that the 1997 budget is rigorous, much more so than the previous budget. Portugal must adhere to European Union targets to belong to the first group of countries to join a single currency," Silva said.
The government has promised a tough 1997 budget with a social conscience. Analysts said the Socialists should pass it through parliament in a vote in November.

Finance Minister Antonio Sousa Franco said on Thursday that privatisation revenues could reach 500 billion escudos ($3.2 billion) in 1997 and that the government would not raise taxes in 1997 for the second straight year.
Guterres said in New York this month that the state could raise 450 billion escudos from privatisations in 1996, well above its target of 380 billion.
The prime minister has said he is determined that Portugal should qualify as one of the first group of countries to join a single European currency by the end of the century.

Silva said he did not expect an acrimonious round of wage talks because several of the negotiators in the government, including himself, were former public sector union officials and knew the people across the table very well.
"People know each other and so they have a greater respect for each other, which didn't happen before (under the previous centre-right Social Democrat government)," he said.
Silva said the government had no plans to reduce the size of the civil service, which he said was no more swollen than the European average.

The government was studying reforms to the present inefficient distribution of civil servants across the ministries and was seeking to end the "precarious" freelance contracts regulating up to 10 percent of civil servants, Silva said.
